title: An Exploration of Attacks on AI Agent Systems
summary: As autonomous AI agents become more integrated into sensitive domains, it is crucial that single and multi-agent AI systems are secured. This paper investigates how prompt injection attacks can exploit both direct user inputs and inter?agent communication to leak sensitive information and trigger cross-agent infections. While our tests mostly highlight key vulnerabilities in single-agent systems, we also extend these attacks to multi-agent frameworks, investigating how weaknesses can propagate across agents. Our findings emphasize the need for more robust defenses as AI agents become more commonly embedded in real-world workflows.

title: SoK: Privacy-Preserving Order Matching
summary: Privacy-preserving order matching enables traders to discover and execute compatible orders while limiting disclosure of sensitive trading information. Existing systems span financial markets and blockchain-based asset exchanges and employ diverse market structures, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions, making their privacy guarantees difficult to compare. We present a systematization of privacy-preserving order matching covering 22 protocol families. We organize the order lifecycle into four phases: order representation and submission, order discovery and collection, order-matching, and settlement, and characterize each phase by protected and exposed information, access roles, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions. Our analysis shows that privacy is not a single protocol-level property: protecting selected order attributes or individual phases does not necessarily prevent leakage elsewhere in the lifecycle. We identify recurring trade-offs among privacy, functionality, trust, and verifiability, highlighting the challenge of achieving end-to-end privacy across the complete order lifecycle.

title: Organizational Context for the Enterprise Security Brain
summary: Agents that investigate and decide on enterprise security reason over a machine-readable view of the environment: its assets, identities, configurations, relations, and findings. The correct judgment about an asset also depends on what the organization knows about it: who owns it, what business function it serves, which policy governs it, and which risks were accepted. Part of this knowledge can be inferred from machine state, such as an ownership tag; most of it is recorded by people in policies, audit reports, architecture diagrams, tickets, and conversations, outside machine state. We call this distance the organizational context gap. Closing it poses four challenges: extracting the right claims from heterogeneous organizational data and, at inference time, detecting claims made stale by live state, checking live state against the governing policy, and binding architecture diagrams, which carry the business logic, to live resources. We introduce organizational context as a layer of the enterprise security brain and define it with a taxonomy and six properties its representation must preserve. We then define a context model in which a claim carries one meaning, an attestation records each source that asserts it, strength is derived from live evidence at read time, and claims resolve onto the entities of the asset graph. On a production environment spanning AWS, Okta, Google Workspace, and GitHub, extraction recovers 0.80 of a pooled 1,355-claim ground truth at 0.87 precision, with 0.5% of extracted claims unsupported by their source. An agent reasoning over live state and resolved context raises the conflict in 0.97 of stale-finding tasks, and reaches answer correctness of 0.83 on policy-alignment tasks and 0.86 on architecture tasks.

title: HOMARD: Hammering Off-chip Memory via Aggregate power Rail Disclosure
summary: Software-based microarchitectural attacks have mainly exploited timing differences to infer information from DRAM. However, defenses and optimizations can prevent timing-based approaches from resolving precise microarchitectural behaviors. We show that unprivileged millisecond- and milliampere-resolution power sensors on modern Arm SoCs can recover DRAM mapping functions and reveal the data dependence of memory accesses without timers. We present HOMARD, a methodology that reads DRAM activity from this telemetry, and two attack primitives. HOMARD-RE is a hierarchy-aware linear-algebraic method that reverse-engineers DRAM addressing functions from power alone. HOMARD-DATA recovers the Hamming weight of a fetched cache line through joint-power rail templating and secret byte values through correlation power analysis on the same rails. Across an AMD ZCU102, a Raspberry Pi 5, and a multi-chip-based LPDDR4 NVIDIA Jetson TX2, HOMARD-RE succeeds where row-buffer timing methods fail. On the Pi 5, HOMARD-DATA classifies 9 Hamming-weight levels at 81.5% accuracy and recovers secret bytes in minutes by correlating rail current with data-dependent bit toggling between neighbors in a row. Both primitives work with an architectural load or a mispredicted Spectre-RSB path on which no value is architecturally read. These results establish unprivileged power telemetry as an independent side channel for profiled microarchitectural attacks, particularly when timing falls silent.

title: Low-Complexity SVD-Based Precoding over Zero-Padded ISI Channels
summary: We propose a low-complexity SVD-based transceiver for zero-padded memory-$1$ ISI channels. Appending a single zero-padding symbol to an $n$-symbol block yields an $n\times(n-1)$ channel matrix with an \emph{exact symmetric tridiagonal Toeplitz Gram matrix}. This structure provides closed-form singular values and vectors, enabling exact SVD precoding and equalization via FFTs without explicitly forming dense SVD matrices. The resulting implementation has $O(n\log n)$ complexity and incurs only a $1/n$ rate penalty. The resulting parallel scalar subchannels enable joint adaptive PAM and power allocation for SER minimization, followed by exact soft-information computation for LDPC decoding. At comparable code rates near $0.945$, simulations show that our proposed scheme outperforms a conventional TX-FFE/RX-DFE system with hard-decision Reed-Solomon (RS) decoding by approximately $5$ dB at FER $10^{-5}$. At high SNR, it achieves nearly the same FER performance as a SOVA-based receiver with LDPC decoding, while replacing trellis-based detection with fast SVD precoding and exact scalar soft-output computation.

title: On the Performance of Randomly Generated Codebooks in Near-Field Communications
summary: Near-field communication with large antenna arrays requires beamforming techniques that account for spherical wavefront effects. While predefined codebooks are widely used in multiple-antenna wireless systems, the performance of randomly generated codebooks in the near-field region has not been investigated. In this work, we study four randomly generated codebooks for near-field communications: random vector quantization (RVQ), random phase (RP), random far-field (RFF), and random near-field (RNF) codebooks. We use the known RVQ gain distribution as a benchmark. For RP, we derive a large-array bulk approximation and characterize the high-gain tail behavior of the gain distribution. For RNF, we characterize the high-gain tail behavior of the gain distribution. For RFF, we derive an analytical approximation for the maximum achievable beamforming gain when far-field beams are used to serve near-field users, along with the corresponding maximizing far-field direction. We also analyze the maximum-gain scaling with codebook size. Monte Carlo simulations verify the analytical results and show that RVQ and RP degrade significantly as the array size increases, while RNF achieves the most favorable high-gain scaling. RFF can outperform RVQ and RP for finite codebook sizes, but its maximum gain saturates below one due to the phase mismatch between the far-field beams and the near-field channel. These results show how codebook structure, array size, and codebook size affect random beamforming performance in the near-field.

title: Minimum Bounding Sets for N-1-1 Branch Contingencies Under Thermal and Voltage Limits in Linear Network Models
summary: N-1-1 contingency analysis studies the loss of one element followed by system adjustments and the loss of a second. The number of contingency pairs increases quadratically with the number of applicable elements, and traditional ranking-based screening methods cannot guarantee that omitted pairs are bounded. This paper determines the minimum bounding set of two-branch-outage pairs: the smallest set that can reproduce the worst value of every violated thermal and voltage limit of a linear network model. In the DC model, effects of an outage pair can be quantified by the extent of the coupling between the outages. The paper measures this by the cosine between the two outages in the network's cycle space, with a bound that splits into one term per outage and is within a near-ideal factor of $\sqrt{1+\varepsilon}$. This argument extends to every linear model in which an outage subtracts a positive semi-definite low-rank term from a symmetric positive definite matrix, with a tight bound and a collapse test. A model with voltage magnitudes is extracted by performing one Newton step on the energy function of the lossless network in rectangular coordinates. A best-first search built on these bounds reproduced brute force on public systems of up to 2{,}869 buses with 130 to 3{,}800 times fewer pair evaluations for flows and 170 to 23{,}700 times fewer for voltages. Gaps in translation to nonlinear models are explored on the IEEE 118-bus system.

title: Topology Construction Algorithms for DECT NR+ in Normal and Ultra-Dense Deployments
comment: 14 pages, 17 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing
summary: The 5G-grade DECT NR+ technology designed to support massive machine-type communications (mMTC) relies on the decentralized mesh connectivity concept. The currently utilized topology construction algorithms are very sensitive to the node density, which causes interference at the node association phase and may lead to instable topologies. In this study, we propose several algorithms that need to be utilized at relay and leaf nodes to allow stabilization of the topology: (i) load-dependent relay allocation, (ii) hysteresis-based association control, (iii) blacklist-based association control, and (iv) smart beacon placement. Due to the complex interference structure in DECT NR+ mesh systems, we utilize system-level simulations to assess the performance in both normal and ultra-dense conditions in terms of the efficiency of topology construction and the performance characteristics of the resulting topology. Our results show that dense DECT NR+ networks do suffer from topology instability, with reassociation rates exceeding 10 per second and recovery times lasting over 10 minutes. By implementing the proposed mechanisms, the network dynamically scales, reducing the number of required relays by more than half, from 34% to 15%. They also stabilize the topology by reducing the reassociation rates to just 2-3 per second allowing large-scale networks of several hundred nodes to operate efficiently.

title: Algebraic Integer Quantization for Machine Learning Applications
summary: In this article, we propose algebraic integer number formats (AINF) as a framework for highly configurable and accurate compressed computation. A key property of AINF is its straightforward reduction to purely integer arithmetic, enabling error-free multiply-accumulate operations. We develop a matrix multiplication engine that exploits this property, obtaining performance within a predictable factor of the most efficient numerical counterparts on modern hardware accelerators. Another key advantage of AIQ is the freedom to select algebraic integers tailored to the numerical characteristics of a given use case, offering optimization opportunities that are fundamentally unavailable in floating-point or fixed-point formats. Motivated by these properties, we introduce algebraic integer quantization (AIQ), a lossy compression format for large language model (LLM) inference, and provide results demonstrating that AIQ achieves competitive accuracy compared to the industry-standard MX format across a diverse set of models and benchmarks at equivalent bit-per-parameter budgets. The experiments presented in this article employ algebraic integers of degree two (quadratic integers); generalizations to higher-order and, in particular, multidimensional algebraic integers promise even greater computational advantages and remain a promising direction for future work.

title: Cancerous Backdoor Attack: Gradual Activation via Invisible Tokens and A Stage Controller
summary: Backdoor Attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) typically follow a trigger-response pattern, where satisfying a trigger condition activates a single terminal behavior. However, this single-point backdoor activation does not explore attacks in which malicious behavior develops gradually through multiple intermediate stages before reaching the terminal activation stage. We present Cancerous Backdoor Attack, that gradually corrupts an LLM's reasoning over a sequence of interactions by leveraging invisible tokens and a stage controller. Specifically, invisible tokens provide hidden stages to the model without appearing in the user's visible request and the stage controller tracks the attack's progression during inference to realize gradual activation. We evaluate Cancerous Backdoor Attack across several reasoning datasets. The attack consistently produces gradual reasoning corruption across models and tasks. We compare Cancerous Backdoor Attack with prior backdoor attack baselines to demonstrate our proposed attack outperforms the baselines. Our results indicate that reasoning corruption can develop gradually before it becomes visible, making answer accuracy alone insufficient for detecting backdoor attacks.

title: Beyond Hypercontractivity: Stronger Communication Converses via Rényi Contraction
summary: We study the relationship between strong data-processing inequalities for Rényi divergences and hypercontractivity. For Rényi divergences of order greater than one, we characterize the contraction of Rényi divergences through a property of the dual Markov operator that we name power contraction. Using the contraction coefficient, we derive an upper bound on rectangle probabilities in terms of their marginals that is at least as strong as the corresponding bound obtained via hypercontractivity. Combining this result with inversion of the binary Rényi divergence, we derive communication lower bounds for one-way communication-assisted agreement distillation. Examples involving binary symmetric and rare-event Z-channels illustrate the improvements over standard hypercontractive converses.

title: Simultaneous Direct and Indirect Channel Estimation for RIS-Assisted MIMO Communications
summary: This paper introduces an enhanced channel estimation method for reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications. Considering the presence of both the direct link from the base station (BS) to the user equipment (UE) and the indirect link \textit{via} the RIS, we formulate a tensor-based receiver for joint direct and indirect channel estimation called the TenDICE algorithm. The proposed receiver relies on an extended parallel factor analysis (PARAFAC) tensor model for the received pilot signals, from which the involved (direct and indirect link) channels are estimated using a simple alternating least squares scheme. The proposed TenDICE method is compared with the state-of-the-art least squares (LS) method, Khatri-Rao factorization (KRF) method, enhanced trilinear alternating least squares (E-TALS), and the theoretical Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) based on normalized mean square error (NMSE) and spectral efficiency (SE). The proposed TenDICE outperforms the LS and E-TALS methods and performs similarly to the KRF methods while estimating the direct channel.

title: Symbolic-Permutation-Based Direct Sparse Jacobian Assembly for Accelerated Power-Flow Analysis
summary: The repeated assembly of the sparse Jacobian matrix constitutes a primary computational bottleneck in the Newton-Raphson power-flow analysis. Through an algebraic equivariance analysis of the Jacobian matrix, this paper proposes a direct sparse Jacobian assembly method based on symbolic permutation. By pre-applying the permutation to the admittance matrix during a one-time symbolic phase, the runtime bus-type projection overhead is entirely eliminated. Consequently, complex Jacobian differentiation and global matrix assembly fuse into a single operation, yielding a single-pass, branchless algorithm that streams values directly into contiguous memory. The framework is realized in the open-source RustPower solver. Benchmarks on IEEE test systems and PEGASE 9241 demonstrate that the proposed assembly is 24.4-30.1x faster than the MATPOWER- style baseline and 6.0-7.8x faster than the Schafer-Braun optimized assembly. End-to-end, the grid-level solve time is 11.7x-154.3x faster than pandapower 3.5.4 with Numba, while leaving numerical results and convergence behavior unchanged. Compared with the native C++ LightSim2Grid 1.0.0, grid-level performance is comparable on IEEE 39 and 1.3x-1.8x faster on IEEE 118 and the PEGASE systems. The method extends directly to general problems where a sparse Jacobian inherits its structure from a static network operator, including transient stability analysis, EMT simulation, and OPF Hessian assembly.

title: PCM: Programmable Congestion Management for Terabit RDMA NICs
summary: Datacenter congestion control (CC) and load balancing (LB) evolve rapidly as workload demands change, but deployment depends on RDMA hardware and transport interfaces. Emerging programmable RDMA engines tie policy code to vendor APIs. Operators must therefore port each policy for every platform they deploy. We address this with PCM, a programming model that separates portable congestion management from platform integration on datacenter NICs. Developers write event-driven handlers that they can debug in simulation and reuse on real hardware. PCM exposes flow telemetry as signals and uses triggers to support per-event reactions and coarser responses to accumulated feedback. Vendors provide optimized backends that map signals and output controls to native NIC mechanisms with defined feedback and control semantics. We demonstrate PCM's expressivity by implementing eleven well-known datacenter CC and LB algorithms. We deploy PCM across four distinct datapaths: an Ultra Ethernet simulator, CPU-based UCCL, and on-NIC offloads on NVIDIA ConnectX-8 and Microsoft 1P. On CX-8, PCM-Swift achieves processing capacity equivalent to one reaction per three 4 KiB packets at 800 Gbit/s, using one-fifth of the NIC's hardware threads. In UCCL, it matches native Swift's 1.56 Tbit/s goodput with 64 KiB chunk-level control. PCM's design informed ongoing Ultra Ethernet work toward a portable congestion management interface.

title: Kairos: Toward a Byte-Level Foundation Model for Every Modality
summary: Small language models trained on a single local machine leave little room for architectural trial and error. Kairos combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention and sliding-window attention over shared projections (LiZAttention2), block-wise Attention-Residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layer and a multi-scale byte-level codec, trained with a uniform-noise denoising objective over one byte space shared by text, image, audio, video, lidar and control streams; this report asks whether the combination optimizes at all before asking whether it is useful. We give code-derived algorithms for each component, including a cross-session recurrent-state memory gate, then run convergence sanity checks: overfittinga single 440-byte sentence at 1--15M parameters, text only, with three seeds for codec and attention choices and single-run sweeps for seven further factors. The two attention variants tested at 3\,000 steps (LiZAttention2 and window attention alone) reach a minimum loss near $10^{-3}$. After 600 steps, the mean minimum loss ranges from 0.018 (patch codec) to 0.354 (depthwise convolutional codec) with an identical ranking on three seeds. An apparent advantage of shared over separate attention projections closes with more steps or more diverse data and reverses when the projections are frozen: it is a convergence-speed effect, not a capacity effect. These checks suggest that the implementation optimizes; they say nothing about generalization, multimodal training or comparison with existing models, which a planned pretraining run is meant to address. The Discussion sizes a 200M-total/25M-active target analytically; none of its throughput figures is measured. Code is available at https://github.com/fabienfrfr/Kairos . Python package at https://pypi.org/project/kairos-fm/ .

title: Enabling Extended SGX Enclaves inside Confidential Virtual Machines
summary:
Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs), such as AMD SEV-SNP, and process enclaves, such as Intel SGX, provide workload protection against cloud threats. However, they strongly differ in TCB, deployment cost and speed, peer workload protection, resource sharing, fine-grained isolation and attestation, and programming capabilities. Nesting process enclaves within CVMs offers an optimal solution and an opportunity to address long-standing SGX limitations: lack of intra-enclave protection, expensive transitions and exception paths, slow enclave cloning, and a restricted programming model that limits Library Operating Systems (LibOS).
  This paper introduces TEEVisor, a CVM-resident architecture consisting of a security monitor and a kernel driver that leverages AMD SEV-SNP Virtual Machine Privilege Levels (VMPLs) to build hardware-protected, process-level enclaves inside a guest CVM with two modes: (1) an SGX binary compatibility mode to run unmodified SGX applications; and (2) a novel extended SGX~(eSGX) mode optimizing slow execution paths and offering richer enclave programming capabilities. On commercial AMD EPYC hardware, against native CVM execution, TEEVisor incurs under 5% overhead on compute- and memory-bound workloads, around 12% on I/O-heavy applications, and accelerates enclave cloning to a rate of 93~$μ$s/MB of enclave size, demonstrating that eSGX semantics inside a CVM are practical for production use.

title: A Ray-Traced Digital Twin for 5G NR Positioning with OpenAirInterface
comment: submitted at 22nd Wireless On-demand Network systems and Services Conference
summary: Evaluating 5G positioning on a physical testbed ties every measurement to one propagation environment and one antenna layout, so any question about an alternative deployment requires a new field campaign. We present a ray-traced digital twin of the GEO-5G testbed at EURECOM that drives an unmodified OpenAirInterface (OAI) 5G stack with per-antenna channels computed by Sionna-RT over a 3D model of the site. The distributed gNB antennas are modelled as independent radio devices rather than as elements of a compact array, which preserves the per-antenna absolute delays on which time-difference-of-arrival (TDoA) positioning depends. With them preserved, the twin drives OAI's SRS-based UL-TDoA pipeline to metre-level accuracy consistent with that reported for the physical deployment. We then use the twin to answer a question the physical testbed cannot. Widening the carrier truncates the tail of the horizontal error distribution without improving a typical position, and leaves the vertical error untouched, because the latter is limited by the array geometry rather than by the measurement. That limit is predictable from the antenna coordinates alone, and a height-diverse layout reduces the RMS height error by a factor of four.

title: Low-Complexity Tensor-Based Channel Parameter Estimation for mmWave MIMO-Assisted Systems
summary: This paper presents a low-complexity tensor-based channel estimation framework for downlink mmWave massive MIMO systems using passive Butler-matrix beamforming. By modeling received signals as a third-order PARAFAC tensor, we exploit known pilot structures via bilinear alternating least-squares (BALS) optimization to reduce computational overhead. The decoupled spatial factors are then processed via 1D and 2D ESPRIT to extract angles of arrival and departure with automatic pairing. Additionally, we derive the Cramer--Rao lower bound (CRLB) for this architecture. Simulations confirm the proposed estimator outperforms conventional least-squares, achieving accurate channel reconstruction and approaching the CRLB at moderate-to-high signal-to-noise ratios.

title: ROAM: Reinforcement Learning Optimized Adaptive Moving Target Defense for Smart Grid
comment: This manuscript is under submission at IEEE TIFS
summary: Smart grids rely on distributed phasor measurement units (PMUs) and wide-area communication networks whose data-acquisition pipelines are vulnerable to stealthy false data injection (FDI) attacks that evade conventional bad-data detection (BDD). Moving target defense (MTD) counters this exposure by continuously remapping sensor identities, but existing schemes apply static or pre-scheduled randomization and are each constrained by a single failure mode: seed-based methods are fast yet fragile to key compromise, while machine learning (ML) based prediction methods are resilient yet incur prohibitive latency. Neither adapts its randomization to live threat evidence. This paper presents ROAM, a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) driven MTD framework in which a deep Q-network (DQN) agent continuously re-optimizes the sensor-to-ID mapping at the aggregation layer. At each decision step, the agent selects the deception coverage, flags the specific sensors to remap, and sets the split of the remapped sensors between seed-based and ML-prediction-based recovery, without modifying PMU hardware and while preserving IEEE C37.118 compatibility. On held-out BDD-compliant FDI scenarios across the IEEE 14-, 57-, and 118- bus systems, ROAM keeps the percentage of stealthy attacks below 3% while sustaining detection rates above 93%. Against an adaptive soft actor-critic (SAC) attacker that observes the defender's configuration, ROAM keeps stealthy attacks below 2.6% with detection above 92%. Hardware-in-the-loop testing on an OPAL-RT platform confirms real-time feasibility, with sub-18ms average shuffle execution and an average reshuffle blind window of 2.6% of the 3-s decision cycle.

title: Configuration Migration Planning through Decoupled Modeling and Searching
summary: Executing large network configuration changes, called migrations, is slow and error-prone today; operators must manually devise a safe order for updating devices that does not disrupt traffic and meets operational intents (e.g., low total time). We develop Smoothie, a versatile migration planning framework that, unlike existing tools, can support diverse operational intents. Inspired by automated planning, it achieves versatility by decoupling the encoding of network safety and intents from the search for a viable plan. Smoothie uses symbolic simulation for general and scalable safety encoding, after which it can use a range of planners, including existing off-the-shelf planners and a new one we developed for optimized parallel plans. We demonstrate Smoothie's versatility and benchmark its performance using diverse migration scenarios on many topologies. It finds both sequential plans and parallel plans, and the parallel ones compress up to thousands of configuration updates into no more than 3 steps. Its versatility does not come at the expense of performance: finishing most planning tasks in less than 1 hour.

title: An Input-Dependent Readout Phase for Resonant Sequence Models
summary: Sequence models with a fixed-size state avoid the quadratic cost of attention, but face a design choice. An input-dependent state transition gives content-dependent memory at the cost of FFT-based training, while a fixed transition keeps the O(T log T) convolutional path but reads memory the same way for every input. ResonatorLM, a recent model of the second kind, reads a bank of damped complex oscillators through a fixed learned phase per head. We make that readout phase a function of the current token, which adds input dependence to the read only, keeps the convolution exact, and costs 0.2 percent more parameters. An analysis of the untrained bank shows that phase does encode elapsed time, but an ordinary token falls below the background within 2-8 steps and no choice of damping extends linear reconstruction beyond about 16 tokens. In 6M-parameter character-level models on WikiText-2, the input-dependent phase matches the original at the training length and removes its failure beyond it: trained on 256 tokens and tested on 1024, perplexity falls from 12.81 to 3.76. We trace the failure to long-memory heads that accumulate more history than training exposed them to. The learned phase tracks the current character rather than distance and does not improve retrieval.

title: PVBRF-ID: Private, Verifiable and Byzantine-Robust Federated Intrusion Detection for Oilfield Enterprise Networks
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables, 3 supplementary tables. Simulation study on public Edge-IIoTset traffic; code and raw results: https://github.com/nawaralseelawi/pvbrf-id
summary: Federated learning allows dispersed oilfield sites to train a shared intrusion detector without pooling network traffic, yet its aggregation step forces a choice between privacy and robustness. Byzantine-robust rules must read each update in the clear, whereas secure aggregation hides updates from the checks that detect poisoning. We present PVBRF-ID, a two-server protocol in which sites secret-share their updates and the servers jointly test each update's norm and its cosine similarity to a reference computed on a small clean root set, revealing one accept bit per site. Commitments, Merkle roots and a homomorphic audit make the inclusion of accepted updates publicly verifiable. On a 15-class Edge-IIoTset task with ten sites holding differently distributed data and ten random seeds, PVBRF-ID matched FedAvg on clean data (macro-F1 0.708 vs. 0.706) and withstood sign-flip attacks (0.696 vs. 0.091). Against an adaptive attacker controlling 30% of sites, PVBRF-ID with secure clipping reached 0.641, whereas FedAvg fell to 0.046; plaintext multi-Krum remained higher by 0.052. An update-inference attacker recovered each site's class mix from plaintext updates (Spearman correlation 0.81) but not from one server's view. Backdoors passed the filter, and noise-based mitigation gave only heuristic protection. The implementation uses Python 3.13, NumPy 2.3, 30 rounds and 10 seeds.

title: Structure-Aware Online Optimization of the Age of Information with Unknown System Statistics
summary: Timely information dissemination is essential in modern communication systems, where low informational latency is critical for networked control, monitoring, and real-time decision-making. The Age of Information (AoI) has emerged as a fundamental metric for quantifying information freshness at the receiver. A key challenge in AoI optimization is selecting the update generation rate: infrequent updates lead to stale information, whereas overly frequent updates increase queueing delays. We develop a structure-aware, data-driven framework for adaptive AoI optimization modeled as single-server queues with unknown system statistics. Our key idea is to exploit analytical representations of the AoI gradient, which depend on a finite-dimensional collection of system quantities that can be estimated from observations collected during system operation. This reduces the online learning problem to estimating the quantities required by the gradient, rather than learning the AoI objective as a black box. We propose an online stochastic approximation algorithm that jointly estimates these quantities and optimizes the update generation rate. We prove almost sure convergence of the algorithm to the optimal update generation rate under mild regularity and moment conditions, despite the temporal dependence induced by the underlying queueing process. We demonstrate the framework in four representative incomplete-information settings, including FCFS queues with unknown service characteristics or hidden background traffic, a preemptive LCFS system with partial observations, and a generate-at-will system with threshold waiting.

title: Multistatic Terahertz ISAC for Object Shape Identification
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to IEEE GLOBECOM 2026 Workshops (Third Workshop on Positioning and Sensing Over Wireless Networks)
summary: 6G networks are expected to sense their surroundings using the same waveforms that carry data. We ask how much can be learned about the shape of an object from the terahertz echoes that user equipment transmissions produce as they scatter from that object on their way to a ceiling-mounted access point, with no sensing hardware beyond the communication link itself. We build a physics-based multistatic forward model at a 300 GHz carrier with 50 GHz of bandwidth, combining Physical Optics (PO) and Physical Theory of Diffraction (PTD) scattering with an image-source multipath lattice, molecular absorption and directional horn antennas. The model makes explicit a property of the PO mechanism hierarchy that is usually left implicit. Six physically distinct mechanisms share only three frequency exponents, so the spectral slope does not by itself determine which mechanisms a target presents and therefore cannot by itself determine its geometry. Angular diversity is accordingly a requirement for identifiability rather than an optional refinement. We compare a transmitter-count-invariant 2D-CNN with a physics-informed RBF-SVM on object orientations never seen in training. Accuracy climbs from roughly 70 percent with one transmitter to 96-97 percent with 20. The CNN gains in two regimes, irregular placement and lossy targets, while on metal under quasi-uniform placement the SVM baseline is fully competitive. Performance falls off gradually under occlusion, holding 78 percent with three quarters of the surface hidden and 63 percent when the classifier has never seen an occluded target. Multi-object scenes are limited by interference between overlapping returns rather than by angular coverage, so presence detection saturates after roughly four transmitters.

title: Distributionally Robust Adaptive Iterative Covariance Steering for Small-Body Proximity Operations
summary: Autonomous small-body proximity operations require continuous-thrust guidance under uncertain gravity, solar-radiation pressure (SRP), and stochastic disturbances. We combine iterative covariance steering (iCS) with $L_1$ distributionally robust adaptive control ($L_1$-DRAC) to provide risk-aware collision avoidance despite mismatch between the nominal planning model and the true dynamics. Iterative covariance steering plans a nominal feedback policy satisfying distributionally robust conditional value-at-risk keep-out constraints, while $L_1$-DRAC compensates for dynamics uncertainty and bounds the residual distributional mismatch through a Wasserstein radius used by the planner. In $\mathbf{1000}$ paired Monte Carlo trials with gravity, SRP, and diffusion mismatch, $L_1$-DRAC adaptive control reduces the keep-out violation rate from $\mathbf{32.7\%}$ to $\mathbf{0.2\%}$ and the physical collision rate from $\mathbf{16.4\%}$ to zero, without actuator saturation.

title: Maneuver Coordination Using V2I to Improve Traffic Efficiency at Intersections
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures, accepted at IEEE VNC 2024
summary: Traffic efficiency and air pollutants are major issues in urban transport systems, as they are critical points for traffic flows and people living in urban areas, respectively. In response to this challenge, connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) have garnered increasing attention, with the potential to address the above challenges through cooperative maneuvering and real-time communication. In this paper, we consider an intersection served by a multi-access edge computing (MEC) where CAVs communicate with a controller to pass the intersection without the need of signals and without stopping unless in presence of heavy congestion. For this purpose, we propose a first-in-first-scheduled (FIFS) algorithm, and we specify the communication protocol for its practical implementation. The solution is validated through simulations with varying traffic densities, showing that it provides significant gains in travel time and emissions compared to both uncontrolled intersections, with or without traffic lights, and a benchmark solution derived from the literature.

title: CircuitTree: Composing Circuits into A Syllable Transcriber
summary: The goal of circuit discovery is to decompose a monolithic neural network into tiny modular subnetworks which are interpretable in the sense that each does an identifiable subtask. We develop a practical method for composing arbitrarily many circuits into a single model. We propose a greedy, density-scaled composition algorithm that overcomes limitations of previous attempts to compose circuits by naive union, then generalize it to $N$ circuits via CircuitTree, a new data structure built on a $Θ(N\log N)$ tree-compose schedule. We compose circuits pruned from HuBERT for classifying individual phonemes into a syllable classifier, a capability none of the 39 phoneme circuits has individually. Chaining CircuitTrees into a hierarchy-of-circuits pipeline, we transcribe open syllables at 64.8\% accuracy, within 1.2 points of a 66.0\% ceiling that shares no circuitry at all, with 99.5\% of circuit components shared.

title: Better Batches, Better Privacy: Random Allocation for DP-BandMF
summary: The current state of the art for batch selection and noise addition in differentially private training is a combination of DP-BandMF (informally, DP-SGD where the noise added in two different steps can be correlated if the steps are within $b$ of each other) and privacy amplification by sampling via Monte Carlo accounting. First, whereas prior batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF were inspired by Poisson sampling, random allocation is known to outperform Poisson sampling for DP-SGD. We therefore propose and analyze new batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF inspired by random allocation, improving RMSE by up to $1.85\times$ over previous work. Second, Monte Carlo accounting typically requires drawing $Ω(1/δ)$ samples from a privacy loss distribution, making accounting costly. We increase sampling and scoring throughput by two orders of magnitude through a carefully optimized GPU implementation. Finally, previous work chose the DP-BandMF strategy matrix and the batch selection strategy independently. We give a simple framework for choosing these parameters jointly, reducing RMSE by up to $13.4\%$ over fixed strategy matrices.

title: Goal-Oriented Ordered Autoencoding for Successive Refinement in Progressive Communication
summary: Goal-oriented communication often struggles to sustain downstream task performance under variable and unpredictable bandwidth. We address this problem by proposing GO-OAE (Goal-Oriented Ordered AutoEncoding), which learns a progressively refinable quantized latent sequence, optimized directly for task utility rather than source reconstruction. Each component of the sequence is represented for transmission by its code index, and the learned ordering enables inference from any received prefix of the index sequence, with performance improving as more indices arrive. We prove that optimizing the goal-oriented distortion objective is equivalent to solving a weighted conditional information bottleneck formulation, and introduce an unbiased multi-prefix importance sampling (MPIS) estimator, to reduce GO-OAE training computational cost from O(BK) to O(Bm) with m << K, and reduces the estimator variance by a factor of 1/m. Experiments show that, on MiniImageNet, GO-OAE achieves over 96% of the lossless upper-bound classification accuracy using 324 bits per image (683X compression vs. raw RGB), and already attains over 94% of the upper bound with only 70% of the transmitted indices. It consistently outperforms reconstruction-optimized codecs and ordered autoencoders trained with uniform prefix sampling across all transmission budgets, demonstrating effective communication at extreme compression rates.

title: Generative Control of Time-Modulated Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces for Scalable Directional Modulation
summary: Time-modulated intelligent reflecting surfaces (TM-IRS) achieve directional modulation by switching their elements on and off at designed instants and durations, so that an undistorted signal reaches the intended user while appearing scrambled elsewhere. We propose a Flow Matching (FM)-based generative framework that designs these parameters for strong scrambling and reliable reception simultaneously. For orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) signals, we introduce a physics-informed reward that maximizes the time-modulation harmonic energy radiated in the null space of the legitimate-user response, subject to a minimum per-subcarrier signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR), without requiring knowledge of adversary directions. Unlike prior generative flow network (GFlowNet) approaches, which assign discretized parameters sequentially, the FM model generates complete continuous configurations jointly, decoupling the generation depth from the number of elements and accelerating training. It also learns a distribution over configurations that can be resampled to vary the scrambling pattern. Numerical results show that, compared with a GFlowNet baseline, the proposed approach reduces the time to training loss near-saturation by $99.4\%$ on average for $3{\times}3$ to $12{\times}12$ surfaces, attains higher final rewards, scales to $80{\times}80$, and confines the low-symbol-error region more tightly around the legitimate user.

title: Closed-loop domain generation enhances battery health diagnosis
summary: Reliable electrode-level degradation diagnosis is essential for accurate health estimation and non-destructive monitoring in advanced battery management. Diagnosis models developed under controlled laboratory conditions can fail when operating conditions change, while acquiring sufficient full-lifespan data in new target domains remains prohibitively time-consuming and practically unfeasible. Here, we propose a closed-loop domain generation framework to enable cross-domain battery health diagnosis under dynamic conditions. Physics-constrained domain generation is achieved through Variational Autoencoder-based latent extrapolation, which maps the source data and few-shot early-life target domain data into a shared latent space and generates cross-domain samples within physical boundaries. Bayesian optimization closes the generation-diagnosis loop by automatically calibrating the sampling, latent regularization, extrapolation, perturbation, and generation-volume hyperparameters using leakage-free development validation, thereby strictly excluding later-life target data from optimization and ensuring the quality and quantity of generated data. Numerical results demonstrate that, across four cross-domain cases, the proposed framework achieves average root mean square errors of 1.53%, 2.15%, and 2.02% for positive electrode active material loss, negative electrode active material loss, and lithium inventory loss, respectively, whereas traditional methods suffer from notably higher errors or even complete failure. This framework provides a general pathway for onboard and physics-consistent electrode-level degradation diagnosis, independent of downstream diagnosis models.

title: On the Alignment Between Spectral Efficiency and Positioning Accuracy in Multi-LEO Clusters
comment: The paper has been accepted for publication in the 2026 IEEE 1st ISAC Conference
summary: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations are expected to play a key role in future 6G Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTNs), where dense deployments enable cooperative multi-satellite processing for communication and positioning. While existing works have addressed communication and localization objectives separately, the correlation and alignment between these objectives remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the correlation between Spectral Efficiency (SE) and positioning accuracy in cooperative multi-LEO satellite clusters. We consider an uplink direct-to-device scenario in which multiple satellites jointly process user signals and evaluate cluster performance using SE and Position Error Bound (PEB) metrics. We derive Time-of-Arrival (TOA)-based and Doppler-based PEBs, while communication performance is quantified through the achievable SE under joint signal processing. Using realistic LEO constellation simulations, we demonstrate that for clusters of seven satellites, SE exhibits a strong negative correlation with Doppler-based PEB (correlation coefficient of $-0.72$). In contrast, its correlation with TOA-based PEB is notably weaker, ranging between $-0.55$ and $-0.37$. These findings suggest that communication-oriented LEO clusters are largely compatible with Doppler-based positioning, but not necessarily with TOA-based positioning.

title: Behind-the-Meter Photovoltaic Visibility from Net Smart Meters: Deployment Regimes and Operational Insights
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the 10th IEEE Conference on Energy Internet and Energy System Integration (IEEE EI2 2026). IEEE Xplore publication pending
summary: Distribution operators need visibility of behind-the-meter photovoltaic (PV) generation, yet most residential customers are observed only through net smart meters. Deep-learning-based PV disaggregation can restore this visibility, but its operational value depends on whether the model serves known customers, new customers, future periods, or new regions. We quantify this dependence using four deployment regimes that separate household transfer from temporal extrapolation, applied to Ausgrid smart-meter data with cross-dataset adaptation to the Pecan Street data. Using a fixed training protocol, we benchmark representative deep sequence architectures for PV disaggregation under regime-matched evaluation. At a fixed 48-hour context length, daylight mean absolute error (MAE) of the best model rises from 0.104~kW on seen households in the future test period to 0.185~kW on unseen households over the same period, and under a fixed training contract the deployment regime explains far more of the error variation than model choice. Under target-domain normalization, fine-tuning on five target-region households reduces source-model transfer error by 28\%--36\%. Long input windows help known-customer extrapolation, while their new-customer benefits vary by model. These findings suggest regime-matched error budgets, limited target supervision for model adaptation in new regions, and use-case-dependent context selection for energy data analytics.

title: Onions in the ATmosphere: Decentralizing Trust in Identity
summary: Multiple approaches have been implemented for identities that associate meaningful identifiers, such as domain names, with self-authenticating identifiers, such as onion addresses. While these approaches offer various advantages both from identifier meaningfulness and from identifier self-authentication, identifier association itself is subject to blocking, hijack, fingerprinting, and other forms of surveillance and manipulation. So too are the resources associated with an identity comprising a meaningful identifier and a self-authenticating identifier. This paper describes ongoing work on two such approaches to self-authenticating meaningful identity (SAMI): associating a registered domain name with an onion address (onion association) and associating an atproto handle with a decentralized identifier (DID association). We present both the application of already implemented and published means of secure onion association to DID association and the combination of both in a single identity. Finally, we describe grounding identity association and integrity in contextual trust, wherein trusting attestations of identity relies on contextual relevance of an attestor to the identity rather than relying only on structural authority, for example as embodied in the traditional centralized infrastructure.

title: Gaussian BROJA Partial Information Decomposition in Closed Form
comment: 28 pages total, including 10 pages of main text, 2 main figures, 5 supplementary sections, and 5 supplementary figures
summary: The BROJA partial information decomposition provides an operationally motivated way to separate the information that two sources carry about a target into unique, redundant, and synergistic components. For continuous and high-dimensional variables, however, computing the BROJA decomposition requires solving a difficult optimization problem. Previous work showed that, when each source-target pair is jointly Gaussian, the problem can be reduced to finite-dimensional numerical optimization. Here, we derive a closed-form solution to this optimization problem, enabling direct computation of the BROJA decomposition in the general multivariate Gaussian setting. The resulting closed-form expression enables speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude for high-dimensional Gaussian BROJA PID. Code is available at https://github.com/brainsandmachines/Eigen_PID.

title: Self-Calibration DOA Estimation for Moving Dilated Arrays with Gain and Phase Errors
summary: Moving dilated arrays (MDAs) can increase the uniform degrees of freedom (uDOFs) while alleviating mutual coupling, but their performance is susceptible to unknown gain and phase errors (GPEs). To deal with this problem, we investigate self-calibration direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation for MDAs with unknown GPEs. First, multi-position observations are phase aligned to construct an equivalent virtual array with an enlarged aperture. Next, the motion-induced relationships among the GPEs are exploited to establish explicit calibration constraints. By leveraging the orthogonality between the steering vectors and the noise subspace, the joint estimation of the DOAs and GPEs is formulated as a constrained optimization problem. To solve this problem, a two-stage alternating optimization (AO) algorithm is developed. In the first stage, the GPEs are estimated in closed form with the DOAs fixed. In the second stage, the estimated GPEs are used to calibrate the covariance matrix, after which the DOAs are refined using the multiple signal classification (MUSIC) algorithm. To obtain reliable initial estimates, a rotational invariance-like (RIL) initialization method is further developed by exploiting two translated virtual subarrays with identical GPEs. Furthermore, the Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) is derived to characterize the theoretical performance limit of the considered system. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method converges reliably and achieves accurate DOA estimation under different array apertures, numbers of snapshots, GPE levels, and numbers of sources.

title: Fast-DeePC: Fast Data-Enabled Predictive Control using Soft-constrained Scheme
summary: Data-enabled predictive control (DeePC) replaces the explicit system model of model predictive control with a data-driven predictor built directly from recorded input-output trajectories, but the original hard-equality formulation keeps its coordinate vector as an online decision variable whose size grows with the offline data length, so the online problem grows more expensive as more data is used to enrich the behavioral representation. This article proposes Fast-DeePC, a framework which relaxes this consistency relation into the control objective with a quadratic ridge on the coordinate vector in place of the customary sparsity-promoting penalty, admitting a closed-form, offline elimination of the coordinate vector and reducing the online problem to a fixed-size box-constrained quadratic program solved by a structure-exploiting interior-point method. On identical soft quadratically regularized problems, the result matches a general-purpose solver's solution and is up to two orders of magnitude faster.

title: RAPID: Proactive Rate Control for Enabling High Data Rate and Low Latency in 5G Edge Networks
summary: Many 6G use cases such as tactile Internet and eXtended reality applications would simultaneously require a high data rate and low latency wireless connectivity.It is increasingly being realized that the current transport protocols relying on packet loss and delay are insufficient to satisfy the data rate and latency requirements of such applications. To address this problem, we propose RAPID, a transport layer solution designed for private 5G edge networks, where the bottleneck is located at the base station. We show that by regulating the send rate to maintain a target physical resource block utilization, we can achieve high data rate, low latency communication. We design a simple yet effective policy that adapts to the dynamic nature of wireless channel conditions. In a multi-UE scenario with two RAPID flows and one TCP Cubic flow, our testbed results show that RAPID flows achieve significant improvements in one-way delay, i.e., 72x and 55x lower compared to TCP Cubic, with negligible packet loss at the cost of modest goodput reductions of 16% and 27%, respectively.

title: GlucoPRISM: Protocol-Supervised Pretraining for Cross-Cohort Glucose Transfer
summary: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) foundation models encode each day as one vector that mixes who the person is, what happened that day and how the sensor measured it, so measurement differences travel with the representation into new cohorts. We ask whether pretraining can place the measurement component that harms transfer in known coordinates, so that deployment drops them with a fixed projection and no target data. GlucoPRISM supervises a GlucoFM backbone with response contracts, rules for how each part of the representation should change when only the day or only the sensor changes: a 64-dimensional Trait band should change with neither, a 48-dimensional State band only across days, and a 16-dimensional Sensor band should track the device. Synthetic sensor views calibrated on paired Dexcom and Libre recordings, different-day pairs and glucose-summary targets supply this supervision without clinical labels. Across twelve cross-cohort directions, dropping the Sensor band from the same frozen encoder raises mean transfer AUROC from 68.75 to 73.57, against 69.3 for GlucoFM. The gain has two parts. Into CGMacros, the one target cohort recorded with two sensor types, filtering adds 11 to 19 points, and this holds when the generator is recalibrated on half of the participants and scored on the other half. On the other eight directions filtering is neutral and the encoder itself exceeds GlucoFM by 3.5 points. The device remains linearly decodable after filtering, so the filter removes a device-related component that harms transfer rather than all measurement information. The retained bands improve window AUROC on thirteen of fourteen public task--cohort cells (Holm-adjusted p=0.031) and correlation on fourteen of fifteen clinical endpoints in an external cohort of 9,303 participants.

title: Power, Performance, and Area of HPC-Based Malware Detectors: An FPGA and Open-PDK ASIC Study
summary: Hardware malware detectors (HMDs) classify programs as benign or malicious based on hardware performance counter (HPC) data. Previous studies have shown that ensemble classifiers outperform other classifiers on detection metrics. However, the area, power, and timing costs of HMDs remain open questions. We address these questions across a comprehensive design space comprising multiple classifier families, variable HPC sets, and ensemble learning methods. We designed a pipeline to reconstruct selected trained models, generate synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) implementations, validate each design against a bit-accurate golden model, and evaluate the implementations. The results show that tree- and rule-based detectors achieve the highest detection performance with nearly an order of magnitude less area and several times lower energy than function-based classifiers. Reducing the number of HPC inputs to fit a processor's concurrent-counter limit preserves detection performance while substantially reducing area, power, and delay.

title: Neural Polar Codes for Source Coding
summary: This paper presents a data-driven approach to lossless and lossy source compression using polar codes. Classical polar source coding achieves fundamental limits with low complexity for binary memoryless sources. However, for unknown q-ary sources with memory, successive-cancellation (SC) decoding requires an explicit source model and can be computationally prohibitive. We present analytical SC recursions and show that exact implementations scale quadratically with alphabet size and cubically with state-space size. To overcome these limitations, we develop neural polar decoders trained directly from data to approximate conditional distributions of synthetic polar coordinates without requiring an explicit source model. These learned distributions enable estimation of entropy rates, mutual information, and rate-distortion functions, and support explicit polar compression schemes. For lossless compression, we identify high-entropy polarized coordinates and reconstruct the remaining coordinates using the learned SC recursion. For lossy compression, we combine neural polar decoders with a neural test channel to estimate and optimize the mutual information-distortion tradeoff and construct an explicit lossy polar code. We also extend the framework to Wyner-Ziv compression with decoder side information by learning conditional polarized distributions and a reconstruction mapping. Experiments on memoryless sources, sources with memory, and real genomic data show that the learned decoders closely match analytical SC decoders when available and remain applicable when conventional methods are computationally infeasible or the source model is unavailable.

title: Lightweight Time-Frequency Vibration Sensing for Consumer Device Condition Monitoring
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, and 4 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Consumer Electronics (ICCE 2027)
summary: Consumer rotating devices, including washing machines, air conditioners, electric fans, robotic vacuum cleaners, and home fitness equipment, increasingly rely on vibration sensing for intelligent condition monitoring and predictive maintenance. Ensuring reliable operation in these resource-constrained appliances requires efficient, lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) solutions capable of processing non-stationary signals under real-world operational interference. This paper proposes a lightweight AI-assisted vibration sensing framework that employs continuous wavelet transform (CWT) and Hilbert-Huang transform (HHT) to convert one-dimensional (1-D) vibration time-series signals into two-dimensional (2-D) time-frequency representations. These representations are subsequently analyzed using lightweight deep learning architectures, specifically MobileNetV3-Small, ConvNeXt-Tiny, and the You Only Look Once version 11 classification model (YOLOv11-cls). Public bearing benchmark datasets, including Case Western Reserve University (CWRU), Paderborn University (PU), and Intelligent Maintenance Systems (IMS), are utilized as representative rotating components to investigate model generalization. The proposed framework is designed with eventual embedded deployment in consumer electronics in mind. Experimental results demonstrate that CWT combined with YOLOv11-cls achieves high diagnostic accuracy, while MobileNetV3-Small provides an attractive low-latency alternative for computationally constrained edge platforms. Conventional random splitting is also compared with dataset-specific structured isolation. The results highlight the importance of avoiding data leakage and quantify tradeoffs in classification accuracy, parameter count, floating-point operations (FLOPs), model footprint, preprocessing cost, and central processing unit (CPU) inference latency.

title: SecFD-FL: Frequency-Decoupled Federated Learning with Secure Aggregation for Charging Load Forecasting in Internet of Electric Vehicles
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Accurate charging load forecasting is essential for the reliability and efficiency of the Internet of Electric Vehicles (IoEV), yet it is challenging on two fronts: charging demand is highly stochastic, and the data collected by distributed sensors is privacy-sensitive. Although federated learning (FL) preserves data privacy, collaborative training still remains vulnerable to an honest-but-curious server that can invert shared model updates to reconstruct private data. To address both data volatility and privacy concerns, we propose SecFD-FL, a frequency-decoupled federated learning framework for IoEV comprising: 1) a dual-stream gated recurrent unit (GRU) network that separately models short-term and long-term charging load volatility, and 2) a lightweight secure aggregation layer for privacy preservation. Specifically, the secure aggregation layer employs a zero-sum additive masking protocol that perturbs each client's upload with high-variance noise, preventing the server from reconstructing private data while preserving the exact aggregate. Extensive experiments have been conducted on both EV-level and charging station-level using real datasets. The experiment results show that SecFD-FL reduces global RMSE by up to 60% over centralized baselines, achieving Jain's fairness up to 0.991 across clients, and reduces DLG-attack reconstruction correlation by 8 times to 15 times relative to FedAvg -- all with no additional per-round communication cost beyond a one-time key exchange.

title: One-Way Delay Model for 5G Low Latency, High Data Rate Communications
summary: Achieving low delay and high data rate communication in 5G requires preventing persistent queue backlogs at path bottlenecks. A key indicator of queue buildup is an increase in one-way delay (OWD) of packets. However, accurately measuring OWD is challenging due to synchronization issues between the sender and receiver. Moreover, using OWD to infer the onset of queueing can be inefficient. For instance, congestion control mechanisms that rely on latency as a congestion signal may result in cellular network underutilization, see, e.g., [1]. Thus, to develop more efficient rate control approaches, it is crucial not only to estimate OWD accurately but also to perform a more fine-grained analysis that provides detailed insights into the queue status. This paper presents a framework for modeling OWD in 5G edge networks, where the wireless link is typically the path bottleneck. %, by modeling it through measurable delay components. We demonstrate that OWD is dominated by queueing delay (QD), particularly at high data rates. We analyze QD by decomposing it into two main components: aggregation delay and channel access time. Aggregation delay can be accurately measured at the user equipment (UE), and channel access time can be estimated based on network conditions. Our key contribution shows that QD, while challenging to measure directly at the base station (BS), can be closely approximated by combining these components. We validate this model through NS3 simulations under varying network loads and single- and multi-UE scenarios. This framework provides a foundation for developing advanced mechanisms for congestion control and bottleneck detection in 5G networks.

title: CacheScope: Exact-Compute Allocation for Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration
summary: Training-free feature reuse accelerates diffusion transformer inference by replacing full denoising computation at selected steps with cached approximations. Existing methods mainly improve the reconstruction of skipped features, but we find that once a stable first-order reconstructor is used, increasing reconstruction complexity brings limited gains, whereas the placement of exact-computation steps has a much larger effect on fidelity. More importantly, absolute shallow-probe variation is jointly affected by input-trajectory displacement and network response strength, and therefore does not directly reflect cache risk. We address this confounding by normalizing probe-output variation with the corresponding input displacement, yielding a directional gain per unit trajectory movement. Based on this signal, we propose CacheScope, which identifies high-risk reuse steps online and selectively falls back to full denoising computation while leaving the underlying cache reconstructor unchanged. CacheScope requires no additional training, gradients, auxiliary networks, or prompt-specific offline schedule optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev, Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, and Open-Sora 1.2, CacheScope achieves up to 3.57x acceleration and reduces median LPIPS by up to 70.1% over the strongest probe-based baseline.

title: Vulnerable Models in the AI Supply Chain: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Propagation, and Usage Patterns
summary: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has established a complex supply chain, but many of these shared artifacts harbor severe vulnerabilities such as insecure serialization and architectural backdoors. While prior efforts have extensively scanned model registries to flag malicious artifacts, a critical gap remains in understanding how developers actually adopt and integrate these unsafe models into downstream software systems. We bridge this gap by conducting a large-scale empirical study on the usage and propagation of 16,977 known vulnerable models on HuggingFace flagged by InsightDB. We track their prevalence across GitHub repositories, software packages, fine-tuning chains, and deployed applications. Our analysis reveals that, despite being publicly flagged, these vulnerable models appear in over 21,000 code locations across more than 5,000 open-source repositories, with 3,757 distinct flagged models (22.1\%) actively referenced in at least one project. To understand how these models are integrated in code and identify recurring usage patterns, we categorize and analyze the recurring patterns surrounding them via a customized pipeline that combines Code Property Graphs extraction with a tailored Frequent Subgraph Mining approach. Across all patterns, we find no evidence of provenance verification or model sanitization logic, with developers frequently bypassing security parameters or delegating trust to permissive framework defaults. These findings underscore that scanning model files alone is insufficient, highlighting the urgent need for context-aware security analysis and stricter integration guardrails at the application layer of the AI supply chain.

title: On Privacy Mechanism Design Under a Bounded $α$-Lift Leakage Constraint with $χ^2$-Utility
summary: We study the design of a statistical privacy mechanism under a bounded $α$-lift leakage constraint. An agent observes useful data $Y$, which is arbitrarily correlated with private data $X$, and releases $U$. The goal is to maximize Pearson $χ^2$-information $χ^2(Y;U)$ while satisfying the point-wise privacy constraint. This utility is an $f$-information that is nonnegative, obeys data processing, and measures the aggregate normalized change from the prior $P_Y$ to the posteriors $P_{Y|U=u}$. The main benefit of this choice is that $χ^2(Y;U)$ is exactly quadratic in the posterior perturbations; hence, no local approximation of the utility is required. For the nonlinear $α$-lift constraint, we derive a uniform Taylor-remainder bound that remains valid for the optimizing, $ε$-dependent perturbation. When $P_{X|Y}$ is invertible, this yields a closed-form quadratic surrogate, an explicitly scaled binary mechanism that satisfies the original $α$-lift constraint, a computable sufficient range for $ε$, and an $O(ε^{3/2})$ bound on the utility gap. For $α=2$, the solution is exact over an explicit range. We transfer these results to point-wise Rényi-divergence privacy, including an exact-feasible mechanism, an explicit privacy-budget range, and matching gap bounds. We also give an exact formulation for arbitrary leakage matrices and evaluate exact-feasible mechanisms numerically.

title: Certified Outage Dimensioning of Fluid Antenna Receivers: Required SNR, Aperture, and Port Count
summary: We study the SNR, aperture, and port count needed to meet a target outage in a single-user downlink with a fixed transmit antenna and a single-RF fluid antenna receiver. For known spatially correlated Rayleigh channels and ideal port selection, a sampling-free residual certificate controls reduced-rank outage error over a continuous SNR interval. Positive Bessel features support large arrays, and bounded importance sampling converts the certificate into simultaneous design intervals. At 1 bit/s/Hz and outage $10^{-5}$, a four-wavelength, ten-port receiver requires 4.40--4.55 dB. Reducing its port count from 256 to ten costs 0.70--1.25 dB under a joint 95\% probability statement. At 3.5 wavelengths, ten ports require 4.90--5.05 dB. Integer-port screening across 3--8 dB shows how aperture and port requirements change with available SNR; an effective-SNR transformation extends these decisions to other rates. The reported intervals include model and sampling uncertainty under checked Gaussian covariance inputs. A constructive slow-growth rank bound and a 16--1024-port study support compact evaluation as port count grows.

title: Virtual Transmission Lines from Data Center Workload Migration: Coordinated Multi-Year Transmission Expansion Planning
summary: The rapid growth of electricity demand from AI data centers is creating a dual mismatch in power systems: a temporal mismatch between fast-rising demand and slow transmission expansion, and a spatial mismatch between concentrated data-center loads and geographically dispersed renewable resources. These mismatches can exacerbate transmission congestion, resulting in unserved data-center load and renewable-energy curtailment. This study models geographic workload migration as a virtual transmission line (VTL) that changes nodal data-center demand without transferring physical electricity. A mixed-integer linear programming model is then developed to co-optimize multi-year candidate-line construction and workload migration, subject to construction delays, renewable-energy curtailment, unserved data-center load, workload-balance requirements, communication-bandwidth constraints, and link-latency limits. The model is evaluated over an eight-year planning horizon on a modified IEEE 14-bus system. The results show that coordinating VTL with physical transmission expansion reduces total system cost, unserved data-center load, and renewable-energy curtailment while alleviating transmission congestion. VTL-aware planning also requires one fewer candidate line than build-only planning. However, VTL alone cannot meet system demand and does not eliminate the need for physical transmission reinforcement. Sensitivity analysis indicates that VTL provides the greatest value when transfer capacity is tight, construction costs are high, load growth is rapid, and data-center flexibility is greater. Additional validation on the IEEE 118-bus system over a five-year planning horizon shows that coordinated planning retains its cost and reliability benefits while reducing physical expansion requirements.

title: Goal-Oriented Bundle Management and Flow Control for Deep-Space Communications via Reinforcement Learning
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Presented at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026), Antalya, Turkey, 5-9 October 2026. Paper ID: IAC-26-B2.5.8-x113206
summary: Deep-space communications operate under intermittent connectivity, long propagation delays, and relay storage constraints. In such networks, the Bundle Protocol enables store-carry-forward communication, requiring relay nodes to manage limited storage and scarce contact opportunities. Relay-side scheduling and dropping decisions are inherently goal-oriented: transmission resources should be allocated to bundles most valuable to downstream mission objectives. Conventional schedulers, such as FIFO, do not explicitly optimize task utility and may provide unfair service across heterogeneous planetary sources. This paper presents a closed-loop modeling and learning framework for relay-side bundle and flow management in a contact-driven deep-space network, where lunar and Martian updates are forwarded through a shared-buffer relay to Earth. We quantify destination-side information freshness using excess age $Δ_i^e(t)=[Δ_i(t)-d_i(t)]^+$, where $Δ_i(t)$ denotes the Age of Information of source $i$ and $d_i(t)$ is a source-dependent delay baseline. Based on this metric, we define a goal-oriented loss that supports source-dependent nonlinear penalties, allowing prioritization according to mission relevance. We formulate relay control as a constrained semi-Markov decision process (CSMDP) and solve it using masked Lagrangian Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Feasibility-aware action masking restricts transmissions to bundles that can complete within the remaining contact window. DTNSim simulations indicate improved age-based utility and inter-flow fairness compared with baseline schedulers. The proposed framework jointly optimizes relay-side bundle scheduling, dropping, and flow control under contact-driven dynamics with explicit fairness considerations across heterogeneous sources.

title: Market Impact Estimation via Causal Foundation Models
comment: In 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF '26), November 14-17, 2026, Milan, Italy
summary: When a trader executes a large order, the relevant question is not \emph{what will the price be?} but \emph{what would the price have been had I not traded?} Market impact is thus a causal quantity, yet classical models (Almgren--Chriss, propagators) regress price on flow, which is biased whenever informed flow moves prices through information as well as trading. We present a proof-of-concept \emph{Causal Market Simulator}: a continuous-time causal prior-data fitted network (PFN) trained on a synthetic market prior in which a hidden informational flow confounds the flow--price relation by construction, with confounding strength an exact per-episode knob. On this prior, the naive estimator's bias follows a closed form we confirm empirically (up to 68\% overestimation), while the PFN tracks the unbiased true-parameter oracle at high confounding. Its \emph{do-ablated twin}, the same model with the intervention inputs removed, collapses onto the pre-window mean. Zero-shot, the model responds at the ground-truth scale to metaorders in an ABIDES limit-order book ($+0.38$ pre-onset standard deviations against seed-replay counterfactuals), and its intervention response replicates on about 2,300 detected flow bursts in BTC/ETH/SOL perpetuals and 3,800 on Nasdaq equities, evidence consistent with, though not proof of, causal transfer. Off-prior the response degrades gracefully, and split-conformal recalibration repairs interval calibration. Transfer hinges on encoding the metaorder as added flow rather than a clamped price level, not on more training. A recurrent state-space variant closes the remaining shape gap: its impact accrues over execution duration where the transformer's stays flat, raising the correlation with measured metaorder impact from $+0.68$ to between $+0.92$ and $+0.96$, at the cost of weaker on-prior deconfounding that traces to the training recipe rather than to recurrence.

title: Sample-Preserving Search-to-Decision Reduction for Noisy Linear Equations over Large Moduli
summary:
The Noisy Linear Equations problem involves finding the solution to a random linear system over a finite field given noisy evaluations. This is a generalisation of various learning problems widely used in cryptography, including Learning with Errors (LWE), Learning with Rounding (LWR), and Learning Parity with Noise (LPN).
  We present a new sample-preserving search-to-decision reduction for Noisy Linear Equations that has complexity $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log q, q/σ)$, where $n$ is the dimension of the secret, $m$ is the number of samples, $q$ is the modulus, and $σ$ is the magnitude of the noise (defined suitably for the kind of noise involved). In particular, this implies search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR that run in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ even if the modulus $q$ is exponentially large, as long as the noise-to-modulus ratio $σ/q$ is non-negligible. Our reduction works for prime moduli $q$. If $q$ is composite, it instead produces a list that contains a small multiple of the solution.
  Prior to this work, known search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR either did not preserve the parameters of the problem (i.e., $m$, $n$, $σ$, and $q$), or had complexity that scaled polynomially with either $σ$ or the largest prime factor of $q$.

title: Fundamental Limits of Covert queueing under Busy-Period Observations
summary: Consider a queueing system operated by Bob, which is intended to serve only jobs generated by a legitimate user, Willie. Willie's jobs arrive according to a Poisson process, and the service times are exponentially distributed. Bob seeks to covertly serve additional jobs arriving according to an independent Poisson process, without Willie detecting their presence. As the legitimate user, Willie is provided with certain statistics of each busy period by Bob. In particular, we consider two statistics: (i) the number of jobs served during each busy period and (ii) the duration of each busy period. We establish that, under either statistic, the maximum expected number of additional jobs that Bob can covertly serve obeys a square-root law. Specifically, over n busy periods, Bob can covertly serve additional jobs in the order of square root of n, whereas any scaling which is above square root of n enables Willie to asymptotically detect the presence of these additional jobs with vanishing error probability. Furthermore, we characterize the scaling constant associated with the square-root law, which we refer to as the covert queueing constant, for each of the two statistics. We compare the scaling constants corresponding to the two statistics and argue that the scaling constant under statistic (i) is no greater than that under statistic (ii).

title: LLM-Assisted Hierarchical Interference Control for Satellite-Terrestrial Integrated Networks
summary: Time-varying aggregate interference from low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites challenges terrestrial-network (TN) protection, whereas conservative control degrades LEO quality of service (QoS).
